Difference Between Invoice, Receipt, Quotation and Proforma Invoice in Nigeria
Stop confusing your clients and delaying your payments. A clear breakdown of when to use an invoice, receipt, quotation, or proforma invoice to accelerate cash flow.

Sending the wrong document at the wrong time is the fastest way to delay your own payment. Yet, every day in Nigeria, talented freelancers, agency owners, and SME founders lose millions to a completely avoidable operational error: document confusion.

When a corporate client in Victoria Island asks for a "proforma," sending them a standard invoice triggers a procurement bottleneck. When a customer on WhatsApp asks for a receipt before their transfer clears, you risk exposing your cash flow to fraud.

Understanding the precise difference between an invoice, a receipt, a quotation, and a proforma invoice isn't just an accounting technicality—it is the architecture of trust. Fast-growing businesses don't just do great work; they operate with absolute financial clarity. If you want to get paid like a premium business, you need to communicate like one.

1. The Quotation: The Opening Move

A quotation (or quote) is a formal proposal of your prices. It is sent before any work begins or any goods are delivered.

Think of a quotation as your strategic pitch. It outlines exactly what the client will get and how much it will cost. Once a client accepts a quotation, the pricing is generally locked in. In a high-trust environment, a signed quotation acts as the green light to commence operations.

  • When to use it: When a client asks, "How much will it cost to rebrand my company?" or "What's your price for supplying 50 laptops?"
  • The Operational Insight: Never start work on an unaccepted quote. Ambitious Nigerian agencies use automated quotes to look professional and weed out unserious clients early.

2. The Proforma Invoice: The Commitment

The proforma invoice is the most misunderstood document in the African SME space. It looks exactly like an invoice, but it is not a legally binding demand for payment.

A proforma invoice is a "good faith" estimate provided before goods or services are delivered. Why does this matter? Large corporations and international clients often need a proforma invoice to get internal budget approval or process foreign exchange (FX) requests through the CBN. It tells the buyer, "If you proceed, this is exactly what the final bill will look like."

  • When to use it: When a corporate client needs to trigger their internal procurement process, or for customs purposes in cross-border trade.
  • The Operational Insight: Providing a clean, instant proforma invoice signals to enterprise clients that your business understands corporate governance. It removes the friction from their procurement team.

3. The Invoice: The Demand for Capital

An invoice is a non-negotiable demand for payment. It is issued after the order is confirmed, and usually after the work is done (or at a defined milestone).

In the Nigerian business ecosystem, your invoice is your most important financial asset. It transitions a transaction from an abstract agreement to a concrete receivable. A professional invoice must include a unique invoice number, strict payment terms, your bank details (or a direct payment link), and clear line items.

  • When to use it: When it is time to get paid. Period.
  • The Operational Insight: The faster you invoice, the faster you get paid. Businesses using InvoiceApp.ng generate unique alphanumeric invoice numbers automatically (e.g., INV-2024-X7B9A) and embed direct payment links, reducing the friction that leads to the notorious "I will sort you later" syndrome.

4. The Receipt: The Proof of Settlement

A receipt is the closure of the loop. It is a written acknowledgment that payment has been received in full (or in part).

Never issue a receipt until the funds have definitively cleared in your account. In a market where fake bank transfer alerts are a real operational risk, your receipt is the final, official stamp of a completed transaction.

  • When to use it: Only after the money is sitting safely in your bank account or wallet.
  • The Operational Insight: Automated receipts build massive goodwill. When a client pays via a gateway on an InvoiceApp.ng invoice, they immediately receive a branded, professional receipt. This zero-touch workflow frees you to focus on growth rather than administrative follow-ups.

Remittance is equally important. VAT collected must be filed and remitted to the FIRS on or before the 21st day of the month following the month of transaction. VAT vs WHT in Nigeria: Which One Applies to Your Business and How to Calculate It
VAT and WHT are two different taxes that confuse most Nigerian business owners. Learn when each applies, how to calculate them correctly, and how to stay NRS compliant.

Every Nigerian business deals with VAT and WHT, but most business owners confuse the two. They apply at different times, to different transactions, and have different rates. Getting them wrong on your invoices doesn't just look unprofessional — it puts you at risk of NRS penalties. Here's the complete breakdown.

What Is VAT (Value Added Tax)?

VAT is a consumption tax charged on goods and services at every stage of production and distribution. In Nigeria, the standard VAT rate is 7.5% (increased from 5% in 2020).

When VAT Applies

  • When you sell goods to a customer
  • When you provide a service to a client
  • On most imports into Nigeria
  • On exports (at 0% for qualifying exports)

Who Charges VAT?

If your annual turnover exceeds ₦25 million, you are required to register for VAT and charge it on your invoices. If you're below this threshold, you may still need to register depending on your industry.

VAT Categories on Invoices

Not everything is charged at 7.5%. The NRS recognizes three categories:

  • Standard Rate (7.5%): Most goods and services — consulting, software, photography, catering
  • Zero-Rated (0%): Basic food items, medical supplies, educational materials, exports
  • Exempt: Rent, interest on savings, financial services, charitable donations

On your invoice, each line item must be categorized correctly. Charging 7.5% on an exempt item is an error that the NRS will flag.

What Is WHT (Withholding Tax)?

WHT is an advance tax deducted at the source of payment. Unlike VAT, WHT is not charged by the seller — it is deducted by the buyer before making payment. The WHT rate depends on the type of transaction.

WHT Rates in Nigeria (2026)

  • 10%: Consultancy, technical services, management fees
  • 10%: Royalties, rent, and leases
  • 10%: Commission and agency fees
  • 5%: Construction and building contracts
  • 5%: Supply of goods (where the supplier is not the manufacturer)
  • 2%: Insurance premiums

Who Deducts WHT?

The buyer (payer) deducts WHT before making payment to you (the payee). For example, if a client owes you ₦1,000,000 for consulting services, they will deduct 10% WHT (₦100,000) and pay you ₦900,000.

VAT vs WHT: Key Differences

  • VAT is charged by the seller; WHT is deducted by the buyer
  • VAT rate is 7.5% (mostly fixed); WHT rate varies (5%-10%)
  • VAT is remitted to FIRS monthly; WHT is remitted by the buyer
  • VAT appears on your invoice; WHT appears on the payment voucher
  • Both must be included on NRS-compliant invoices

How to Calculate VAT on Your Invoice

Example: You're invoicing a client for ₦500,000 of consulting services.

  1. Subtotal: ₦500,000
  2. VAT (7.5%): ₦500,000 × 0.075 = ₦37,500
  3. Total: ₦537,500

The client pays ₦537,500. You remit ₦37,500 to FIRS as VAT.

How to Calculate WHT on Your Invoice

Example: The same client deducts 10% WHT on the ₦500,000 consulting fee.

  1. Gross amount: ₦500,000
  2. WHT (10%): ₦500,000 × 0.10 = ₦50,000
  3. Net payment: ₦450,000

The client pays ₦487,500 (₦450,000 net + ₦37,500 VAT). The client remits ₦50,000 WHT to FIRS on your behalf.

Common Mistakes Nigerian Businesses Make

Mistake 1: Charging VAT on Exempt Items

If you charge 7.5% VAT on rent, interest, or basic food items, you're collecting tax you shouldn't. The NRS will flag this.

Mistake 2: Not Including WHT on Invoices

Even though the buyer deducts WHT, your invoice should show the WHT amount. This helps with reconciliation and NRS compliance.

Mistake 3: Using the Wrong WHT Rate

Using 10% WHT on a construction contract (which should be 5%) creates discrepancies that the NRS system will catch.

Mistake 4: Not Remitting VAT on Time

VAT must be remitted to FIRS by the 21st of the month following the transaction. Late remittance attracts penalties.
